original_question: Does the reverse-mathematical strength of the rainbow Ramsey theorem for the Rado graph coincide with the reverse-mathematical strength of Sauer's canonical partition theorem for colorings of a fixed finite graph inside the Rado graph?
target_in_paper: The draft is aiming at the paper’s Rado-graph reverse-mathematics problem comparing the canonical-partition theorem with the rainbow Ramsey theorem. The nearest official formulation is the question, posed most explicitly in the nearby precursor source, of whether the canonical-partition statement (Corollary 4.3) is stronger over RCA_0 than the rainbow-Ramsey statement (Theorem 5.2), with the Rado graph singled out as the main example.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the main objects: the Rado graph, reverse mathematics, the rainbow Ramsey property, and Sauer-style canonical partitions for copies of a fixed finite graph. It also correctly frames the issue as a comparison of strengths rather than as a purely combinatorial existence question.
missing_details: The paper-faithful base theory is over RCA_0; your draft does not mention the base system.
The nearest official formulation asks whether the canonical-partition statement is stronger over RCA_0 than the rainbow-Ramsey statement, not whether the two strengths coincide.
The rainbow side must specify k-bounded colorings (typically for each k >= 2), rather than arbitrary colorings.

The rainbow statement is about colorings of copies of a fixed finite graph (or finite induced substructure) inside the Rado graph and asks for a subcopy of the Rado graph on which the coloring is injective on those copies.

The canonical-partition side needs the exact notion of canonization: after passing to a subcopy of the Rado graph, the coloring is constant on each canonical/strong-similarity class of copies of the fixed finite graph.
The canonical classes are those arising from Sauer’s coding-tree/strong-similarity analysis; this hidden structural notion is essential to make the canonical-partition statement stand alone.
Your wording does not say that the substructure found must itself be isomorphic to the whole Rado graph.
Your draft omits the quantifiers over the fixed finite graph F and, on the rainbow side, over k.
The paper’s nearby context first poses the comparison in the broader setting of homogeneous binary simple structures, with the Rado graph as a special case; your draft suppresses that context.
If one wants the exact Rado-graph specialization from the nearby discussion, the paper separately highlights the edge-coloring case as an especially concrete instance.
refined_question: Over RCA_0, fix a finite graph F and let R be the Rado graph. Compare the reverse-mathematical strength of the following two principles: (1) Sauer’s canonical partition theorem for copies of F in R, namely that for every finite coloring of the copies of F in R there is a subgraph R' isomorphic to R such that on copies of F inside R' the coloring is constant on each canonical (equivalently, strong-similarity) class supplied by Sauer’s theorem; and (2) the rainbow Ramsey principle for R, namely that for every k >= 2 and every k-bounded coloring of the copies of F in R there is a subgraph R' isomorphic to R on which the coloring is injective on copies of F. In particular, is the canonical-partition principle stronger over RCA_0 than the rainbow-Ramsey principle?
justification: The draft is close in topic but not in exact formulation. The official nearby question is not framed as an equality/coincidence problem; it is framed as whether the canonical-partition statement is stronger over RCA_0 than the rainbow-Ramsey statement. The relevant canonical statement is Corollary 4.3, which canonizes colorings by strong-similarity type, and the relevant rainbow statement is Theorem 5.2, which yields rainbow copies under k-bounded colorings. The same source then explicitly asks this reverse-mathematics comparison in Questions 6.2(1)-(2), with the Rado graph singled out in the concrete edge-coloring case. The given arXiv note 1808.10227 is a very short problem list, and the most precise accessible official wording of the problem your draft is targeting is therefore the Questions 6.2(1)-(2) formulation together with Corollary 4.3 and Theorem 5.2.
